author: RosieCampbell
text: I think both are valid points, but some examples better support (1) which is the stated "Copenhagen Interpretation of Ethics", and some better support (2), which should ideally have its own name/post

author: RosieCampbell
text:
In sum, I think there are two different observations in the post:
1. It's bad to get mad at people for doing something even if that something isn't maximally effective
2. It's bad to get mad at people for offering a trade that involves a sacred value if it's consensually accepted

author: RosieCampbell
text: I think the SXSW and PETA examples better support what is perhaps an implicit secondary claim in the post: "if someone consensually accepts an offer, they believe the offer will improve their life, and we should support that even if it involves a sacred value"

author: RosieCampbell
text: By "our distaste for quantifying sacred values" I mean putting a number on them, giving them finite value, weighing them into trade-off calculations

author: RosieCampbell
text: @PTetlock defines a sacred value as "any value that a moral community implicitly or explicitly treats as possessing infinite or transcendental significance that precludes comparisons, trade-offs, or indeed any other mingling with bounded or secular values"

author: RosieCampbell
text: Again, I don't think people were angry that this isn't maximally helpful, they were angry because they perceive PETA to be taking advantage of someone's misfortune to further their own agenda. That feels icky.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Another example given is when PETA offered to pay the water bills of poor families in Detroit if they went vegan for 30 days.

author: RosieCampbell
text: In this case, I don't think people were outraged because it wasn't the maximally helpful thing. People were outraged because it feels demeaning to pay homeless people trivial amounts of money to provide WiFi to wealthy tech people. It's trading dignity (a sacred value) for money

author: RosieCampbell
text: The next example is: In 2012, some homeless people in Austin were given WiFi hotspots so they could offer SXSW attendees WiFi in exchange for $20 per day plus donations. It was labeled a "darkly satirical science-fiction dystopia...a completely problematic treatment of a problem"

author: RosieCampbell
text: I think this is a real and unfortunate phenomenon! However, I think some of the other examples in the post actually point to a different problem, which deserves a post of its own: our distaste for quantifying sacred values, even in consensual trades

author: RosieCampbell
text: This is illustrated well by the first example: In 2010, New York chose some homeless people to take part in a program, and tracked those not in the program as a control group...

author: RosieCampbell
text: The idea is, if you try to do something good, you will be criticized for it not being maximally helpful, even if it was better than nothing. And so people are incentivized to not even try.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Jai Dhyani's "Copenhagen Interpretation of Ethics" says "when you observe or interact with a problem in any way, you can be blamed for it" https://t.co/piEMR6UwQi

text: @StefanFSchubert I guess this is true if people find out they've been lied to? But if a Noble Lie is really successful, people might never realize

author: RosieCampbell
text: So while in theory, a well-chosen Noble Lie *could* have a better outcome, the chance that you will choose one that outperforms the truth out of all the options is very slim,

author: RosieCampbell
text:
Then the reasonable part of their reaction is the only part we can know how we're affecting.

Given this model of public reaction as reasonableness + noise, accurate information will overall lead to better outcomes

author: RosieCampbell
text: If we assume that we're very bad at predicting the ways in which the public will react unreasonably to our message, then we might as well model their unreasonableness purely as a noise term we have no control over

author: RosieCampbell
text: It feels like a Noble Lie involves messing with a complex, delicate system and if you try to interfere with one part it has all these second order effects and unintended consequences (kind of like messing with prices in a market)

author: RosieCampbell
text: But clearly institutions are bad at guessing how people will behave, and bad at 4D chess. It does seem like whenever they attempt this, it would have been better if they'd just been honest

author: RosieCampbell
text: Sure, if the pubic is reliably very smart and reasonable, we would expect that giving them accurate information would lead to better outcomes (setting aside weird game theory dynamics like hoarding goods). But most people don't think of the public as reliably smart and reasonable

author: RosieCampbell
text: In the set of possible things an institution can say, there is: A (the truth), B (a partial truth), C (another partial truth), D (an outright lie), and so on. Of all of these, why should we assume A will generally lead to the best outcome?

text: My god I am grateful that I have a spare room, that I can work from home, that I have helpful friends and family and an understanding boss, for podcasts, for medicine... Being this sick sucks, but I am so lucky in so many ways

author: RosieCampbell
text: I am probably going to be more cautious for a while, either until we have more effective vaccines for the new strains, case numbers go way down, or it's been long enough that I can face the idea of being this sick again 😩

author: RosieCampbell
text: I really, really, don't want a round three. But I also don't want to put my life on pause 😭 Suggestions appreciated

author: RosieCampbell
text: I was hoping that even if I was sick to get out of bed, I might at least be able to be somewhat productive on my laptop. Unfortunately most days I've been pretty useless - just lots of sleeping and podcasts.

author: RosieCampbell
text: People seem to have wildly different experiences of covid, I wasn't sure if that was due to different strains, viral load, individual reactions... I've been struck by how similar my symptoms have been each time, which makes me think the "individual" component is  significant

author: RosieCampbell
text: Even after I recovered from my first bout of covid, I would feel occasional fatigue and chest tightness. I'm still really hoping this is only temporary; I'm not sure how catching it again will affect this 😢

author: RosieCampbell
text: If someone is picking it up for you from the pharmacy (which they should since you shouldn't leave the house) they need to take your ID, and they should probably take a printout of the prescription and the creatinine test just in case

author: RosieCampbell
text: Both times I got Paxlovid. It is disgusting. I used to take it right before bed, but I would wake up in the middle of the night due to the lingering foul taste. Now I take it just before eating dinner so that the food masks it.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Both times, I moved into the spare room, tried to leave it as little as possible, and when I did I wore a mask. My partner who I live with didn't catch it from me either time! So don't give up hope if someone in your house catches it.

author: RosieCampbell
text: Last time, I tested negative over and over again for days, despite having confirmed exposure and severe symptoms. This time I tested positive immediately. I don't know what to make of this.

author: RosieCampbell
text: The worst symptoms for me have been: myalgia, feverishness, fatigue, breathing difficulty, painful cough, sore throat (like a spike/golfball). I haven't had any loss of taste/smell

author: RosieCampbell
text: I am triple vaxxed and thought if I caught covid I'd have a pretty mild case. Not so. I thought the fact that I'd had it only recently (less than three months ago) would make this time around less severe. Not so.

author: RosieCampbell
text: @Gurdur @ciphergoth My feeling is that even without this kind of deliberate self-alteration, an increasingly capable system optimizing for its initial goals would carry significant risks if we don't think through carefully what those goals should be and how we can correct it as it gets more powerful

author: RosieCampbell
text: @woj_zaremba @MaxIlse @OpenAI @sama @Miles_Brundage There's also the factor that those are very high-stakes domains, where mistakes are incredibly costly, and so ironing out kinks and safety issues in lower stakes domains can be valuable

author: RosieCampbell
text: @ciphergoth @Gurdur My guess is "deliberate" is the keyword here - i.e., even if it writes the code for a successor AI, it has no reason to change its goals unless it develops its own intentions (i.e. is self-conscious)? (@Gurdur please correct me if I'm misunderstanding)

author: RosieCampbell
text: @Gurdur @ciphergoth (And even if we manage to ensure it only does what it's used for, there's the question of what risks we take on in the case that people with malicious intent (or even just a lack of good judgement) get control of such capable systems)

author: RosieCampbell
text: @Gurdur @ciphergoth I think of it more as a system that will ruthlessly optimize, and unless we successfully build in safeguards it doesn't seem unthinkable that it could get out of our direct control. Similar to our economic system, or the effects of optimizing for engagement, or the internet

author: RosieCampbell
text: @Gurdur @ciphergoth Curious if you see self-consciousness as a necessary component for AI to be risky? I'm agnostic on the issue of sentience but I still think very capable systems carry significant risks
